And so again, it's -- it's troubling from that point of view, and perhaps at the end of all of the maps if the Prosecution could at least have an opportunity to make some remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. I see no problem with that. Let's move on to map 6.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Map number 6 shows the distribution of forces of the BH Army and the HVO in April 1993. The BH Army attacks Konjic on the 13th of April, 1993. It attacks Vitez on the 15th of April, 1993. In Zenica we have some disarming. The BH Army is disarming the HVO and expelling the people. The conflict in Sovici and Doljani was on the 17th of April, and in that same month of April we have a preparatory attack by the BH Army on Mostar. The green lines still facing the VRS are being held by the BH Army and the HVO, and we have this small portion that they're holding at Stolac, the unit that was called the Bregava Unit. And then we see up here in Bihac, Orasje, and Sarajevo the positions there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next map.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Map number 7 relates to May 1993. On the 9th of May the BH Army attacks in the town of Mostar, and from the 1st to the 30th of June there's an all-out general attack by the BH Army in Konjic. And three small enclaves remain. We can't draw them in here, but we spoke about them. I took part in pulling out of Kostajnica. And that was the situation, but nothing changed. The HVO and the BH Army still co-operated both in Stolac, in the defence against the VRS. This area is held by the HVO. This was held jointly by the HVO and the BH Army precisely as the blue and green lines indicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Map number 8.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Map number 8, number 1. From the 4th to the 10th of June, 1993, the BH Army attacks at the HVO in Travnik, takes control of Travnik, and the soldiers and civilians fled across Serb portions. And we had a chance to see what this looked like on the tapes. The army was disarmed and negotiations were held. Between the 13th and the 15th of June, 1993, the BH Army attacked Kakanj and took control of it. And then from the 1st to the 30th of June it continued to attack Konjic, and the people, the population withdrew, except for small enclaves. So that was the situation. Travnik was taken control of, Kakanj, and the action continued, the operations continued along the other lines. The HVO and the BH Army still acted together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Map number 9.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shows exactly what the situation was on the 30th of June, 1993. The BH Army had taken control of Travnik. That was on the 10th of June. Kakanj the 15th of June. This was crossed out. Kakanj's crossed out here. The BH Army then in Mostar does what we needn't talk about any more. That is to say, the HVO soldiers who were Muslims, of Muslim ethnicity, disarmed the Croatian soldiers, and in Stolac, in an ambush, killed 26 men, established a new line here -- actually, the HVO set up a new line facing the BH Army and the VRS. As I was saying, the BH Army took control of positions north and south of Mostar. South of Mostar up to Blagaj and northwards right up to Konjic, and now the BH Army was taking over the positions facing the VRS, the red line. The HVO, from Blagaj -- takes positions from Blagaj in Mostar along the Bulevar, Antic Street and so on and further on as the map shows, the BH Army and the HVO. We'll see this better on map number 10. This is July 1993, that is to say the point in time when I arrived. We had an attack on Fojnica and the BH Army attacked and took control of Fojnica. The BH Army also attacked and took control of Bugojno. The BH Army attacked Gornji Vakuf and ended it's operation in Konjic, and the line in Mostar remains as you can see here through Cabuna and Vram Planina. The VRS facing the BH Army, the BH Army facing the HVO, the attack in Konjic, the attack in Fojnica, the attack on Bugojno and the attack on Vakuf and that's when the offensive began. As to the other positions in Bihac we still have the BHO -- the HVO and the BH Army together in the whole Tuzla region, the HVO with its brigades was together with the BH Army as it was in Sarajevo fighting the VRS. Do you want me to go on? This is the 30th of July. It is map number 11. The situation in the area under BH Army control and the HVO's control, on the 30th of July 1993. Vitez and Busovaca remain, Kiseljak and Kresevo, Vares, Zepce, Usora, and small enclaves around Konjic. All the rest that is has been crossed out, Bugojno, et cetera, Konjic, Kakanj, Fojnica, Zenica, Travnik, all that is in BH Army hands already, because it was implementing its plan to extend its territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, turning to map 11 coloured in blue and in green, green is the BH Army, and red is for the HVO. On this map we see that there's a part under control by the HVO, which is essentially below, and then there are HVO enclaves in zones that are under BH Army control, it being clear that everybody, all the forces are encircled by the VRS indicated in red; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour Judge Antonetti.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I am looking at this map, and I note that you have identified areas monochrome, and the legend speaks of areas under control of ABiH and HVO. Now, during cross-examination the question has come up quite a number of times about areas under the control of the HVO, and you have consistently persisted rather strongly and said there were no areas under the control of the HVO, but only a very small strip along the front line. Now, this appears -- there appears to be a contradiction which I think you would wish to straighten out.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, this is a map which shows what the BH Army controlled, the Muslim representatives and the Croatian representatives. When I say under HVO control, I'm not -- I don't mean the army. I mean the power and authority there. The HVO was facing the VRS lines, Tomislavgrad, et cetera. Here south of the Mostar towards the Croatian border and within the frame of the BH Army here in these areas around Tuzla, Orasje, and so on. There are two terms, HVO control as an institution and so on. That's one term, and that's what I'm using here. Everything else that's not green and blue is controlled by the army -- well, it's not the Army of Republika Srpska, it's the authority that that represented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This is still a bit puzzling, because as far as Bosnia and Herzegovina, let's say the Muslims, are concerned, we only see here ABiH, and A stands for army. So are you saying that when you paint it green that is an area controlled by the Muslim Army, and when you paint blue that is not controlled by the HVO army but by some other HVO authorities? I watched you and it looked as if you had given an answer. I don't -- I'm not quite sure. Have you given an answer to this midway or -- and if so, what was it, because it's not transcribed.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, Sarajevo was controlled by the authorities in Sarajevo, the Presidency. Now, the BH Army and the VRS come into contact along the lines of contact. When it's green this means the authorities controlled by the Muslims. Here the authorities, along with all the agreements, are the Croats. The army is at the point where the green and blue come into contact and where the blue and red come into contact and where the green and red come into contact, green being the BH Army, blue being the HVO, and red being the VRS. So let's not mix these armies up, and let's not confuse them with the civilian authorities, the civilian authorities protected by their armies at the borders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, you put "ABiH" here, and that does lead to confusion. I don't think that I am to blame for having raised this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Would I like to ask you, Mr. Praljak, about the following, that the -- up to now I haven't seen very well where the Posavina region was situated, and here you have under XI, XIa, you have several enclaves here in the first part number 5, Usora, I'm not sure if Usora was in the Posavina region or not, but then Usora is not mentioned in the second part of that clarification, that is under XIa; and, therefore, of course, I see the Sava and Bosanski Brod, but of course, it is far away from the regions which you, yourself, refer to. So I am a bit at a loss as far as the situation with that particular part, Posavina, which was also which -- from which we have had as well witnesses. So I would like you to point out where those -- I saw your hand that it is probably -- that very small blue region which is rather difficult to read, that part. That is only that one which remained from Posavina according to you, is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I mean under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour Judge Prandler. That remained under HVO control. And why didn't I put an enclave here? Because it is adjacent to the Republic of Croatia, and you could go there. You could take that route. But I'm afraid that there is a bit of confusion here. This part that is being defended together which the HVO and the BH Army, it's also called Posavina. So this is Posavina -- well, you can see that the corridor was forged here, and here from Brcko and the rest, this is Posavina that is being defended by the HVO and the BH Army, and there are HVO brigades which are under the command of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak, next map, please.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Map number 12, well, as you can see, the situation in Bihac remains the same. In Posavina the Posavina on the Croatian side the situation remained the same until the end of the war. And this is the situation as of the 8th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where the BH Army took Travnik, Kakanj, Fojnica, Bugojno, and, in the end, Vares as we were able to see in late October 1993. And the enclaves of Busovaca and Vitez remained, and the area around Kiseljak. Zepce was still there as was this area here from the south of Mostar. And in the BH -- the VRS actually is holding the lines against the BH Army and against the HVO. Here it is attacking. Here the HVO is holding the lines against BH Army, and here in the Tuzla region, the joint forces, to the greater extent of the BH Army and the lesser extent the HVO is holding the lines against VRS and also in Bihac and in Sarajevo where we have one brigade each.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the situation on November 8, 1993. Next map.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is then map number 13. That is how I'm going to mark it. Map number 13 is the same thing that we have seen before, but now things are a little bit more precisely marked here. So it's a bit clearer in military terms, but it's a little bit difficult to discern it. So the Republika Srpska Army and what the BH Army and the HVO managed to defend. And now if we may --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Just for the record, it looks like beginning with 13, we don't have English translations, at least not of 13, and we're going to object to anything that does not have translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, could you read in your own language what is on this map so that the interpreters can translate what is on the map.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, Your Honours. I didn't ask for translation. That's the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina in April and May 1992. Red, that's the areas controlled by the VRS. Green is the territory controlled by the BH Army. Judge Trechsel, I'm saying this colloquially so please don't. And the territory controlled by the HVO is marked with blue. That's the usual way of marking things. We move on to map number 14. We do have the translation. That's situation -- well, we've looked at this map. It's the deployment of the JNA, its armies and corps. The 1st Army, 2nd Army, 7th Army, the Naval District, that's the VPO. And that's the armed forces of the SFRY, the territorial deployment within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, this is map number 13 or is it map 14? I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fourteen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Map 14. Very well. This is a map where the JNA was fully deployed in all the former Yugoslavia in 1985 with the different army corps called 9A, 5A, 7A and 2A, and 2K, and so forth; is that it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. A is army, K is corps, and VPO that's the naval district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That is map number 14.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we move on to map number 15. In 1987, Your Honours. This is very important. The Yugoslav People's Army changes its entire territorial structure and deployment in line with what it would be required to do in order to accomplish the Serbian objectives, and that is a new military district is formed, the naval district remains the same. The 5th Military District is set up, but it's important that the 1st Military District now encompasses the area that corresponds to the borders of Greater Serbia. So as early as in 1987, the foundations were laid for all that and it was all organised in order for this developmental plan that this area from Karlobag to Karlovac and Virovitica can be taken as part of this military district. Can I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that on map number 15, the JNA modified or changed its entire structure. Now, on this map we have 1.VO written, and you also indicated the borders of Greater Serbia, and you're telling us that this was a plan, a plan to attack Croatia; is that it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only on Croatia. Bosnia and Herzegovina is also here. So is Montenegro and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the microphones that are not in use please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Map number 16 shows the aggression of Serbia, Montenegro, and Bosnia and Herzegovina on Croatia. When I say Bosnia and Herzegovina, I mean the forces that were deployed there. I mean the Yugoslav People's Army is actually attacking. I don't have anything to add. Everything is accurate here so the 3rd Corps, the 2nd Corps, the 31st Corps, and this is the plan how from Serbia and from Bosnia and Herzegovina. So in all those directions, and of course with the use of the navy, the destroyers. They destroyed Split and Dubrovnik as the aggression on Croatia was launched in 1991. This is map number 17. It's the same thing, but here I marked two things. It was of particular importance for the Yugoslav People's Army to take Kupres and then to reach Split via Livno and also to go down the Neretva valley in this area to be able to destroy Dubrovnik, to cut it off and then to move in the other direction in order to conquer all of Dalmatia. In 1991, this marks the beginning of the implementation of the plan. Map number 18, that's the operative development of the armed forces of the SFRY in 1992. You can see here that after their defeat or after their retreat of the Yugoslav People's Army from Slovenia, the 31st Corps was moved here. The 14th Corps was moved here. And the 13th Corps was moved to Montenegro where it then proceeded to move to Eastern Herzegovina carrying out attacks here. The 10th Corps, after taking the Knin area and then left it to the local forces, moved to Bosnia and Herzegovina. The 9th Corps, again, after taking the Zadar hinterland and Sibenik hinterland moves to Bosnia-Herzegovina and launches its operation against the Republic of Croatia in 1992, and by that time, they already started attacking Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 1992. Could you please tell us which month in 1992? You're telling us that the 14th Corps is returning as well as the 31st, the 13th, and the 10th, but which month was that, in May? in April? When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are the developments up until March 1992. In March 1992, everything was already in place for the final strike on Bosnia-Herzegovina. You will see that on the next map. That's map number 19. Here you have a quite specific date. It's situation in March 1992. And here you can see the positions of the 13th and 9th and the 10th Corps. They moved first from Slovenia, well, from Slovenia the 13th and the other two from Croatia, and here you see the disposition of the corps within Bosnia-Herzegovina or on the border with the Republic of Croatia and you can see it is designated quite clearly, the number of volunteers and the number of soldiers in each corps. Well, I didn't translate -- have that translated. Well, soldiers are soldiers, and volunteers are those who volunteered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, when we see here the Dobrovojacka, that is the volunteers in each of those brigades or corps, et cetera, mentioned here under 10, 5, 17, 9 and 4, I believe. And of course there are that one even more, that is 13 and the 2nd square mentioned here, so then what I would like to ask you is that the volunteers were to come from the territory concerned that they were deployed, or they were volunteers, let's say, from Montenegro or from -- from Macedonia or Serbia itself. So were there volunteers from over the rest of the republics, or they were mainly based on the Territorial Defence units. That is my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour Judge Prandler, these are the units of the Yugoslav People's Army marked as such. The volunteers came from all over the place, from Montenegro, from Serbia. Serbs naturally from Bosnia-Herzegovina. They came from Croatia. Simply put, Serbs who felt that they wanted to participate in the implementation of the political goals, they volunteered to join the army and their numbers grew.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all the microphones that are not in use please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Map number 20. Your Honours, this is just --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, I'm sorry. I would like to ask you to read out the 3D numbers that you have marked on each map. Each map is in e-court and it's marked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I think Madam Nika that we can add it later on so that I don't waste my time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well it would be easier for people to follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can see quite clearly which map is which. Your Honours, this is what was happening between January and April 1992. Bosnia and Herzegovina was suddenly chock full of Yugoslav People's Army units. You can see the military districts here and you can see what belonged to which military district. All the corps are listed here. I think it's quite clear and there's no need to elaborate any further. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next map.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the next maps, the maps that follow, the map number 21, well, it specifies the overall strength of the JNA and the VRS in the period between January and April 1992, and you can see how in 1992 and 1993 the strength increased. So here when you say personnel, that means soldiers, tanks, armoured personnel carriers, and armoured fighting vehicles, and artillery, cannon. Well, these are the figures. I didn't have this translated because I thought -- because it seemed to me that -- well, that's map number 22. That's the 10th Corps. It's deployed in Western Bosnia. It's under the command of Major General Spiro Ninkovic. You can see the strength, soldiers, volunteers. This is all 1992. The 4th Corps is located in Sarajevo. It's under the command of Major General Vojislav Djurdjevac, the number of soldiers, the number of volunteers and you can see the composition of the units. There is also map 23. For the 5th Corps in Banja Luka, for the 9th Corps at Kupres. Map 24 is 17th Corps located in Tuzla. Major-General Sava Jankovic. The number of men, the brigades, et cetera. So there we have it as regards that territory. At the beginning of 1992, what the disposition of forces was of the Yugoslav People's Army and the volunteers in Bosnia-Herzegovina, who the commanders were.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all the microphones be switched off, please, which are not in use. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How they were armed and so on. I don't understand were there is such a lot of interference and background noise. It seems to be better now. Unfortunately this copy, well, it's not a good copy but it's map number 25. I've already shown this on a clearer map. It is 1993, Operation Neretva 93, in fact. I have nothing more to say about that. Everything's been said. Now, this is the -- from October to November 1993. The number of the map is 26. The situation in the Mostar area is what this map depicts. It's turned round the wrong way. Map 26. Could you all take up map 26 and take a look at it. It's 3D03724. And in red is the BH Army this time, an attack in the Mostar area, Bijelo Polje, and so on and so forth. The axis of attack by the MOS. Unfortunately, you can't see those arrows on this copy, and I can't do anything about that, but it's quite clear, as far as I'm concerned, in the copy I have. It's a bad photocopy, but it says where the attacks were. Well, I don't really know. I can provide you with the original maps or provide the Judges with the original maps perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Place the map on the ELMO, please, because no one can see it. Put it under the ELMO. The October/November map. That's the Neretva operation. It's not that one but the next one.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you would please explain the numbering system, 1, 2, 3, 4, all the way through 10. Say the number of the map.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of the map is map number 26. Here we have it, 26, and that shows the situation as it was in Central Bosnia and moving south in October and November of 1993. And the BH Army attacks are marked in numbers -- or, rather, the Muslim forces. That's number 1. Number 1 shows that. Why is this happening now? 1, Mostar, Hum, Rodoc. 1, here it is; 2, Bijelo Polje, Rastani; 3, Dreznica, Vrdi; 4, Neretvica, Hudotsko, Slatina; number 5, Hare, Uzdol, Prozor, Rama; number 6, Voljevac, Crni Vrh; number 7, Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf; number 8, Voljica, Raduski Kamen; number 9 is the attack on Vitez; and number 10, the attack on Travnik and Nova Bila. Novi Travnik and Nova Bila. That is map 26. And the same thing on map 27, which is 3D -- no, we haven't got 3D here. It's map 27. Also October and November, but showing the axis of attack. Red the MOS. The armed forces of the BH republic are in blue. The main roads are in yellow. The diversions on the roads are marked with these circles here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Praljak. You were somewhere out of the reach of the ELMO right now. If you could show again and taking the map up a bit. We didn't see where you went with your pencil.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The red.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly. No, you must move the map a bit, because this is exactly what we cannot see. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge Trechsel, Your Honour, I'm in a hurry. I don't know why I'm hurrying for goodness sake. I don't know. I just seem to speed up for no reason at all and then this is what happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Praljak, and I'm trying to assist you by pointing out something which you do not see. So do not take it wrong. There's no reproach for once in what I say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, if you would please indicate the legend, the caption. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The red arrows on the map indicate the axes of attack of the Muslim armed forces, MOS, and at the time, well, it was no longer the BH Army. We began calling them the Muslim forces. The blue denotes the defence lines of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The yellow on the map denotes the main roads so that you can see where the main roads were. And let's start with the south. From the coast Ploce, the roads that all the convoys of humanitarian aid passed through, Mostar --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic. General Petkovic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a technical problem. Perhaps General Praljak is a little tired, but you can't have two markings for the BH Army forces, one more MOS and the other for the BH Army. The blue is the HVO, and somebody placed the letters RH HB. So the blue refers to the HVO in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. Petkovic. That is right. The blue is the HVO. I don't know why I read it out differently. And on that map, you can see quite precisely where the BH Army was attacking the HVO. There were two enclaves remaining. This is one. This is another below Zenica. So the Novi Travnik enclave and the Kiseljak enclave. Here we have the BH Army and the HVO. The HVO is blue. And we were attacked from all sides. The red circle here with this cross, the red circle with the cross was the slaughter in Uzdol near Prozor that occurred, the massacre. And here these two Xs are the diversions alone the roads, especially at Stolac where crimes had been committed in the rear. We saw those dead people in the barracks in Grabovina and the previous 26 people who were killed and brought there. And this map is a precise map showing the situation in October and November with the BH Army attack on two enclaves in Central Bosnia that had been broken up, and in Vares -- no. This is Zepce. Vares is over here. So Vares was being taken control of, and the whole of the southern part of the territory is being attacked, is under attack towards Mostar. Konjic has been completely taken control of. And that's the situation in October and November, and that was map 27. We've seen this next one. Now we can move on to what Your Honour's interested in, which is where -- we're going to call this map 28. So this is map 28, and it comes with a translation. It's a plan of attack on the Republic of Croatia after the withdrawal of the JNA from Slovenia, but here we can also see the plan of attack on Dubrovnik, the south, Ploce, Split, Sibenik, Zadar, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I don't have that map. I only have one left, this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the Prosecutor does not have that map.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these are the maps which the General marked following your request, and the Registrar had them printed, and we put them into six groups. We didn't print out the maps, we just sorted them and put them together. So perhaps the Prosecutor doesn't have that particular one, but it does have a 3D number, which means it should be on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I do have it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is map 28. The axes of attack by the aggressor, that is to say the Yugoslav People's Army, and that's what the arrows show. The interrupted blue -- dotted blue line is the line along which the aggressor retreated, not being able to take control of Croatia. The red arrows indicate the different types of obstructions set up by an organised defence throughout the territory of the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. And another important thing is these red circles which denote the garrisons which the JNA were -- had in Croatia and were blocked by the Croatian forces. At the request of the international community, Your Honours, in 1991, Croatia, the Croatian Army, the Croatian armed forces, were forced to deblock the JNA barracks in the Republic of Croatia, and all the weaponry went to Bosnia-Herzegovina pursuant to demands from the international community, which I'm -- if I might be allowed to add was a completely incomprehensible act for anybody to knows the situation on the ground. Anybody who knew what was happening knew what these actions would lead to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Praljak. I would like to clarify an issue of -- on map number 28, which is a very nicely -- I must say it's a really nicely done map. There are two types of legends here. In the one that is inserted in the map, it says: "Possible directions of attacks of the aggressor's forces according to estimations and available data." And on the right-hand side, under number 11, it says: "Plan of the attack to Croatia." Now, these are clearly, I think, two different things, and I would like to know which is the one that we should rely on.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two things at two different times, Judge Trechsel. So according to available information, and I consulted the book by the General, the JNA Army general, and showed which -- what their preparations were and what they intended to do. Now, on the basis of the information we had, we forecast what the attack would look like on the Republic of Croatia, and that's what actually happened. It actually took place. So both. You have both things here, the attack that was forecast, the deployment of JNA forces and so on, and then everything came into being. Everything happened as is indicated on this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That is a third eventuality, namely description of something that actually happened. It is not a plan but a historical presentation of what happened, and that is, I understand, what we should take it as.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Map 29 shows what we managed to do, and it describes the situation. It describes what the BH Army -- or, rather, the VRS managed to do. Martic's army, if you want to call it that, the army set up by the Serbs within the Republic of Croatia. They did not succeed in implementing their plan, but they did manage to take control of this area here. It says the Zone of Rebellion. That's what we called it. The rebel Serbs led by the JNA took control of Vukovar, Baranja, Western Slavonia, that is. They took control of Eastern Slavonia but did not manage to move to the Hungarian border. They took control of everything below Zagreb, Sisak, and then the hinterland of the Adriatic, Sibenik and Split, and the south of Croatia below of Dubrovnik, and to the south and north above Dubrovnik. But they did not manage to take control of the town of Dubrovnik itself and didn't manage to break through to Peljesac or the Neretva River valley, either towards the south and Ploce or the west towards Split. And as far as Bosnia-Herzegovina is concerned, it says very rightly here the HVO, precisely along this line here that I've drawn, set up a defence and managed to stop the JNA's -- the JNA from moving forward, and this happened towards the north of Metkovici. So within -- a few kilometres within the BH Army borders there was some Croatian Army, but the HVO managed to stop everybody here. Of course we could draw in the same for Posavina, but this is the situation as it was in 1992 in the south. So up until this line at the very borders, the HVO managed to stop the breakthrough. Later on they would move towards Dubrovnik and liberate that portion, and everything north of that was held by the HVO. Of course, later on it was joined by the BH Army, or rather, there were a great many Muslims within the HVO who took part in all this. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next map.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Map number 30. It's the situation in this area in 1992 and 1993, and I claim, Your Honours, again as I have explained, on the 10th of April, 1992, a single unit from the 4th Guards Brigade came here into three villages, Tepcici, Slipcici, and another one near Citluk to stop and -- put a stop to an advance of the JNA. A total of 159 soldiers. They came together with me on the same day, because that area was completely empty, and I couldn't man it with anyone. There simply were not enough people. In 1992, that HV unit was in this area from the 10th of April, 1992, until the end of June 1992, and it took part in the operation to liberate South Mostar. After that, it returned to the Republic of Croatia. It was the 4th Battalion of the 4th Guards Brigade stationed in Split under the command of a young officer, General Krsticevic. He went on to command a brigade and was one of its most notable commanders. Here where it's marked with number 2, the Croatian Army was stationed along the Croatian borders. And here between numbers 3 and 4 and down towards Dubrovnik, it was all the Croatian Army. Of course, it was after the signing of the agreement on co-operation in the border areas between Dr. Franjo Tudjman, President Tudjman, and President Izetbegovic, and the HVO held TG2, what His Honour Judge Trechsel asked me. It's the Tactical Group 2 which manned positions from the area south of Stolac towards the Croatian border, defending Neum, among other things. And here we from the HVO and the Croatian Army quarreled over who actually had to hold this line, because this is not a defence line of anything in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is the defence line of Croatia facing the attacks by Republika Srpska. And the Croatian Army did man those positions after a while, but then the international community complained, and the HVO went on to man those lines again, although it is still not clear to me. I would not have complied with it because the Croatian Army in some areas, maybe a kilometre or two, because of the lay of the land and in light of the laws of war, moved into Bosnia-Herzegovina territory towards Dubrovnik. But it was never a part of any conquests. It was just in accordance with the rule that you have to and you can stop an attacker in the tactical depth. And the border facing Dubrovnik was such that you can actually fire on the town from a pistol. So if you want to repel the artillery so that they can no longer target this town, and it is in -- at the territory of another state which is not under the control of the government, because from the beginning of the war, the government in Sarajevo did not have any representatives, any idea how to defend it. This was people organising themselves, and after all, I, myself, in an effort to defend the basic things in life, your mother, your son, your child, friends, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please get back to what's at hand, because you're straying. Please move to the next map.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. Number 31. Map number 31. That's 3D03741. Again, this is the plan of -- for the attack of the JNA and the VRS to the south -- attack on the south of Croatia from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Here you have the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think the number is 31 rather than 51 as you wrote.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 31, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, is it time for the break? I thought it was about 5.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still have five minutes to go. General, please write down 31, because, indeed, we have 51.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thirty-one. So these are the axes of attack by the JNA and the VRS, the attack on Livno towards Split, taking of Kupres, and then from Mostar, they're moving towards Makarska. They're linking up their forces, and we don't have to add anything to it. It's crystal clear as it is. Here we have two maps, 32. Map number 32. This is the map from 1995, operations between the 8th of October, 1995, until the 11th of October, 1995. HVO, HV, BH Army in operations -- operations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, this is not covered by the indictment. What is the point of talking of a situation taking place in 1995? What is the military purpose of giving us this information?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a military point of view, this is what is important: We have to see when the Croatian Army -- when, and what occasions and to what extent actually had a presence in Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the previous map I showed you that it was in the south of Croatia -- or, rather, the Dubrovnik area, A, B, only the unit of 159 people, from the 10th of April until the end of June around Citluk, and the next time there is a regular presence by the HV was in 1995 when Bihac was liberated and when the Croatian troops, the HVO, the HV, and the BH Army together advanced towards Banja Luka. These are two maps. These operations were under the command of General Gotovina. This is southern movement, and you can't really see it here. I wrote Jajce. Jajce was liberated, Sipovo, Kljuc and so on. This was after an agreement that was signed - this is important - by Dr. Franjo Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic about military co-operation. So in 1995, I am --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. It is outside the scope of the indictment, and the General's not even qualified to talk about this. He's not even in his position in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, if I may -- if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one minute. Let me respond to what he said, to what Mr. Stringer said. I can answer any question that I like. That is my answer. General, I asked you a question: Is this useful? You said, Yes, because it shows in 1995 HVO and -- and HV led a joint operations under the command of General Gotovina. We know that. You've said it now we can move on to something else. Mr. Karnavas, what did you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS

utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you told us that in 1995 there was a joint action between HVO and HV. We have the map. Very well. We take this into account. utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]

utterances.text: Last map, 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer, the Trial Chamber consider it fair for you to be able to put questions to Mr. Praljak on these maps if you believe that, according to you, some of these maps can be challenged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the way I understand our agreement with Ms. Nozica, she is supposed to start first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Well, we stuck to the order that is usual for the cross-examination of General Praljak. Now I would like to ask the usher to hand out the binder with the documents to everybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, since I have only 15 minutes, I with like to start with the document -- and I have the feeling that somebody has their microphone on, so it's a little bit difficult for me. utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: At page 14 of the transcript today, in lines 4 through 7, you were asked by my learned friend Mr. Stringer whether Mr. Stojic, as regards to the procurement of the equipment listed here and the payment of medical services to the XY side, did play a logistical and financial role, and you confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that probably -- that he probably had. I didn't confirm it. I said he probably had that role.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, as regards to this document, let us please look at page 2 of this document. I did indicate the document, and I think that the General knows what document I'm talking about. utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that with a high degree of probability.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Likewise -- well, we've all received this document from the Prosecution. utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm it because that's what it says here. We owe the money. Well, I can't confirm that I know that, but as I was able to do that before, I can say that it's highly probable that this explanation is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, let me now put to you a conclusion that was broached here in the courtroom. It is recorded at page 24641 in the course of the testimony of Witness EA. I'm not going to go into any detail so that we don't have to go into private session, but I'm sure that you will be able to recall. The amount that was mentioned was 1 million German marks to be used to pay the equipment and materiel and to pay for the medical treatment for the people from the Kiseljak enclave on -- that was provided by the Republika Srpska Army because the enclave was surrounded at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, and I knew that. There's a high degree of probability that I did know that at the time that they had started doing that, and this is what I said here. And I said that they managed to gather most of the funds for this kind of services.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. That's how it was said here in the courtroom in response to your questions. Mr. Praljak, now I would like us to move on to the document that I've announced. It's the first document that I was going to use in my re-examination. That's P5104. Mr. Praljak, you were questioned about this document at length, and on the 2nd of September, 2009, here in this courtroom, at page 44305, you answered about this document, and the next document, which we don't have to look at it but I will announce it, it's document P5188, this would be your order, and my question to you, Mr. Praljak, is this: Item 1 in this order issued by Mr. Boban, does it pertain to the army? And let me read it: "All units of the armed forces of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna are duty-bound, as they have so far, to wage exclusively a defensive war in order to protect the integrity of the Croatian area, the people living there and material goods and all the natural resources."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That pertains to the armed forces of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, that particular item.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I will have the same question again for the second item, and it reads --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me, a linguistic problem. You have said "exclusively a defensive war." We do not have the "exclusively" in the translation. Perhaps if you read number 1 out we have the translation and can check whether it says "exclusively" or whether not.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let me read again, and it says -- it says "only," perhaps not "exclusively." "All units of the armed forces of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna are duty-bound, as they have so far, to wage only a defensive war in order to protect the ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, let me move on to the second item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, in your own language, when you say "only," does this mean that there's no other possibility; whereas, if it was exclusively, something else could be possible. So when you say "only" in this text, does this mean that it is the only possibility, that no other possibility is available?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Boban drafted this, but the way I interpret it is in the spirit of our language, and that would be precisely what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Item 2 reads: "In the execution of all combat operations, members of the armed forces of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna are duty-bound to abide by the standards of International Law of War and humanitarian law, and I designated the commanders at all levels of command and control as persons responsible for that." Mr. Praljak, although it is quite apparent, I would still like you to answer my question. Does this item of this order again pertain to the armed forces of the HVO HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, now we can only have a quick look at this document, P5188. You are aware of it. We all know what this is all about. You testified about this document on two occasions, and this is the document for which you said that you had forwarded it to all operational zones as is indicated here, to all the units subordinate to the Main Staff and the chief of the military police. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, now I would like to show you three documents that show how this order was forwarded. Could you please look at P5199. That's our next document. Have you been able to find it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is a document issued by commander Miljenko Lasic, Operational Zone South-eastern Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, somebody signed in his stead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite obvious. And you can see here that he paraphrased your order in his order, and you can see who it is addressed to. Is that so? And you can see that the order by President Mate Boban is attached to it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, was this the way in which it was forwarded?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously that's how it was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to look at document 3D915. It's a document that was used by my colleague, Mrs. Pinter, while you were talking about those documents. Have you been able to find it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, this is a document -- I don't want to testify, so could you please tell us whom was this addressed to, what operational zone? You can see that from the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operational Zone North-western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And you can see from the document that this order, your order and Mr. Boban's order, were also sent to the Prozor Forward Command Post, to the brigades Petar Kresimir, Petar Tomislav. L-a-r-d-p-z-o, Tomislavgrad, 6th Military Police Battalion [Realtime transcript read in error "tomorrow"], Tomislavgrad the 5th, Posusje Brigade, Posusje and so forth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now I would like you to look at another document. We have an error in the transcript. The last word was not battalion tomorrow, but let me just check. It was -- let me go back. It was the 6th Posusje brigade. So that was my last word at page 82, line 16. The last document is 3D1104. This is a document from the command of the Operational Zone Central Bosnia, and you can see from it it was submitted to all the HVO brigades, to independent units in the Central Bosnia Operational Zone, to the 7th Battalion of the military police and the Travnik police administration, and it says: "Pursuant to an order of the commander of the Main Staff on the implementation of the order by the president of the HR HB, Mate Boban, which is attached to this document." And then Mr. Blaskic issues his order. Do you agree with me that this is again is an order that we were talking about? So Mr. Boban's order, and your order that is also related to it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the numbers are a bit mixed up. Could you please repeat them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: 3D1104. That should be your penultimate document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, to avoid any questions later on, in item 5 of this order another order is referred to from the operative zone of Central Bosnia, dated the 2nd of August, 1993. Now, so that we have absolutely no dilemmas on this score, I have prepared that order too, and it is P3885, which speaks about the control to stop the convoy. Just so we're clear on what item 5 is about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel Blaskic issued this on the basis of my own order saying that they don't have the right to stop UNPROFOR vehicles from going through and how they should behave.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And it is P3835. That's the number of your order; right? Thank you, Mr. Praljak. That's all I had in my redirect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you, Your Honour, and everybody else in the courtroom. Let me start off by saying good afternoon, Mr. Praljak, officially, and now I have been given permission to ask you a number of questions linked to a document that was shown you by me learned friend Mr. Stringer and the number is P10960, and that's the number under which you were shown Professor Jankovic's report or analysis. Now, I have a few questions for you in that regard. To the best of your knowledge, was Professor Jankovic on the territory of Herceg-Bosnia in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all the other microphones be switched off, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With a great degree of certainty I can say that he was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, Professor Jankovic, was he in Herceg-Bosna in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a great deal of certainty, I state that he was not. I am completely unaware of any such fact, and I think that I would have had to know about it. No, he was not on the territory of Herceg-Bosna. Professor Jankovic was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, did Professor Jankovic ever see or physically touch any pieces or weapons that he analysed in the report we had in front of us?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. His knowledge comes from his work as a professor, not by having an insight into the actual state of the artillery pieces in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, are you telling us that Professor Jankovic, then, did not in fact know what artillery pieces they had in Herceg-Bosnia, but he made his conclusions on the basis of some theoretical premises, looking at the type of weapon, the date of manufacture and so on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite certain. He was judging on the basis of what -- the subject he taught but certainly he didn't see -- have an insight into the weaponry that the HVO had in 1992 and 1993, and in the Croatian Army he dealt with scholarly work concerning the manufacture of weapons, the training of crews, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, General, to the best of your knowledge, Professor Jankovic was he in possession of any documents perhaps linked to these piece -- artillery pieces, firing tables, corrections made and adjustments made to the firing and firing tables or concrete documents related to concrete artillery pieces on the territory of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly didn't ask me for any such documents, and it is also quite certain that I didn't have those documents in my possession, so I can say with a great deal of certainty that he did not have access to those documents. He did not have them before him in writing up his report, because his expertise was not compiled on the basis of an insight into the fact, in the present tense, when it was actually happening on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, Professor Jankovic, did he have a list of soldiers and officers who were deployed in the HVO on artillery positions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely exclude that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does your answer imply that Professor Jankovic, in fact, didn't know at all what specific men were involved, who was in the artillery of the HVO, what these people's training was, what training they had undergone, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He certainly couldn't have known any of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, just one more question in this connection. To the best of your knowledge, did Professor Jankovic talk to any soldier or officer, who in 1992 and 1993 or 1993, was deployed in the artillery of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such case.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. Now, staying with this topic, the artillery, I have several questions just to see what your understanding is of certain rules of warfare as an HVO commander in the second half of 1993. Tell us, please, General, do you happen to know that it was prohibited to attack or bomb a town, village, or settlement which was not defended, that is, that all attacks on undefended localities were prohibited.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that perfectly well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you another question that you would say argumentum a contrario. Do you know that an attack is allowed on defended places?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm perfectly well aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question, Mrs. Alaburic is a little bit complicated. She is asking whether you know that you cannot attack a village, an undefended village. It's very interesting question, and it's merit is that it has been asked, but does this mean in your mind that the army that is about to attack or not to attack knows in advance it is defended or undefended? Do you need to know whether or not the village is defended or not. If one of the belligerent parties doesn't know whether or not a village is defended, can it preventively, after having taken all the necessary precautions to make sure that there are no civilians present, launch a first military operation to conquer the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Judge Antonetti. You cannot take control of a village that -- or attack a village that is not defended. So before you enter a village or pass through a village, for that matter, you do two things: First of all, you collect intelligence, military intelligence; second -- secondly, you reconnoiter. You reconnoiter from some vantage points to ascertain whether along a certain axis there are -- there is an enemy. And thirdly, there is forced reconnaissance work. You send reconnaissance men, one, two, or three, and they advance until they are fired at. Now, there's a rule that holds true in cases of that kind. You can't learn where the enemy is unless you lose some reconnaissance men. So usually these reconnaissance men come across an ambush, and they're killed, these scouts, but it's important to send these scouts out to see the positions of the enemy, and I did this in the Konjic operation together with the BH Army, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know -- and I'm going to refer to the case of Vietnam. In some villages there were apparently some civilians, but in fact, troops were hidden under floor boards or in galleries, underground galleries. In that case, the US Army would send scouts, as you just said, but they wouldn't leave it like that. As soon as they saw a hole, they threw a grenade in it. Is this part of the soldier's manual, who, when he knows that in a village there are civilians, must check to see if some enemy soldiers are hidden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only through forcible reconnaissance, that is to say passing through the village. You send somebody through the village, and if he's not shot at, then most probably there's nobody in the village. They can, of course, search a certain number of houses. Now, the Vietnam War was a specific one. There was a lot of digging and so on when the French were there. That wasn't the case in our parts. So you send two or three scouts to reconnoiter the area, to reconnoiter a village to see the lie of the land, so to speak. And to be quite frank, those scouts were very often killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, in your opinion, in an attack on a defended locality, is it absolutely forbidden, consciously, to attack civilian targets, or is that allowed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not allowed to attack civilian targets unless they are in the service of any military activities by the enemy side.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'll take that a step further. Tell us, please, General, to the best of your knowledge, at a point when a civilian facility is used for military purposes, then that civilian facility becomes a military target; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. There's no dilemma on that score. That's how things stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry for the intervention. Mr. President, this is nothing but legal principles that the Trial Chamber doesn't need to be instructed on by a witness, and there's nothing in these questions that relates to the context of any of the conflicts or crimes that are alleged in the indictment. It's pure law, and the Trial Chamber is the master of the applicable law and doesn't need instruction as it's getting in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right from a strictly legal standpoint, the Trial Chamber has not instructions to receive, to know what the applicable rules of law are. But we have seen a document from Colonel Blaskic that incorporates the order from Mr. Boban on the Geneva Conventions and so on. So one might raise the question as to what is the knowledge of the HVO commander on the rules of law and the international conventions especially insofar as in any worthy army there is a minimum amount that is taught to officers and soldiers as to compliance with rules of war, whether it's the treatment of prisoners or other. So perhaps General Praljak is not, himself, a legal scholar, that is what he said himself, but he does have a minimum of knowledge as to what is allowed and what is not. So I fail to see where the problem lies. Mrs. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am really asking General Praljak these questions in his position as commander. At what point should you launch an attack on a defended locality, whether it is more important to safeguard civilians and civilian facilities or to achieve a military objective. So in view of these concepts and evaluation of interests from the aspects of military interest, is the topic of my re-direct to General Praljak. Now, the fact that these questions have certain legal repercussions and consequences at this point in time, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. The way you have now formulated the question is really asking what the law is, and that the Prosecution is correct in saying that's not the purpose of direct or cross. I have a feeling that you want to demonstrate something else, namely to what extent the witness was knowledgeable of that law. That is a different aspect, and that is correct, but you should then put your question in a way which makes it clear that you do not want to have him tell the Chamber what the law is, but you want him to demonstrate how much he knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, most probably you're right, and most probably, I fail to formulate my question properly, and if so, I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, General, I'm asking you questions as a military commander about attacks on a defended locality, and it's up to you to weigh up all the relevant factors and decide whether you're going to go ahead or not. Now, your last answer, as far as I remember, was to say that never, under no circumstances, is it permitted to target civilian targets, but then you said that if civilian targets are used in -- for military purposes, then they become military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. I apologise again for the interruption. It was my understanding that this -- the scope of this examination relates to the Jankovic report, which relates itself to HVO artillery, use of artillery. So perhaps for the record, if counsel could specify that we're talking about artillery operations on civilian targets versus infantry operations, which is something different and which would be outside the scope, I think, of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, for the moment I'm talking about attacks on a defended locality, and the next step would be to take a look at what civilians are exposed to in an infantry attack compared to an artillery attack and what the possible differences are in the conduct of an army during an infantry operation and an artillery operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic, the problem is as follows: You said, "I will be asking questions based on the Jankovic report." This report addresses the issue of the bridge. I thought you were going to ask questions about whether a bridge can be a military target. Now you are moving to another sphere, field, that of villages with civilian population. The Jankovic report does not cover this. Why are you deviating from the original topic? And the OTP is raising that in his own arguments. He did not raise this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there are two reports written by Professor Jankovic. One relates to the Old Bridge, and that is not the topic of my re-direct. The other one, the other report, is the one which the Praljak Defence never tendered officially, and through an oral decision of yours, you allowed the Prosecution to use it. And I'd just like to remind you that the Petkovic Defence objected and said that it was a new piece of evidence. However, you decided that questions can be asked based on that new document. And now my questions relate exclusively to that second report by Professor Jankovic, which was never tabled as an expert report, and according to General Praljak, it should not have been examined in this courtroom, but since your ruling allowed this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General Praljak, a question linked to that second report now, and that is the question of proportionality during an artillery or any other kind of attack, for that matter, on a defended locality. General, please tell us, do you know that under the principle of proportionality possible civilian casualties and damage to civilian facilities in any attack on an undefended locality must be significantly smaller than the military effects achieved by an attack on the undefended locality? Have you ever heard of the greater importance that is given to the achieving of a military effect then on the -- which must be then much greater than the civilian casualties, or is it the first time that you hear it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, 30 years before the war started, out of curiosity, I studied wars from Napoleon on. I studied all the relevant books, and I focused precisely on this issue: What is the proportion? And I could speak about this for hours with all the facts that I have in my head; how in every war that follows the number of civilian casualties increases: The Vietnam war, the Iraq war, the Israel and Palestine conflict. This has been the subject of my interest for years. I know that, and I presented many of the facts to the Judges already. So I claim that I knew that. I was perfectly well aware of that and this is one of the most difficult military conundrums ever since it was first introduced because you have this principle of proportionality under the law, and that is why we applied this rule very restrictively, absolutely restrictively. So the Old Bridge was a military target, and when they attacked and -- on around the 20th of September when they launched this large-scale offensive, we, in the HVO - and I can claim on the basis of everything that I read in the books - we were the only side that would not have destroyed the bridge. Well, all the armies destroy bridges as they retreat. They burn the bridges behind them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I can just sum up your answer. So you are aware of this proportionality test, and you applied it as the commander of the HVO; is that so? Could you please just very briefly answer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we applied it restrictively, madam. So 20 military facilities were in the centre of Mostar. They were military targets, command posts, headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go through all that with our witnesses, but one last question, General Praljak. Is it your position that at the time when the BH Army started using the Old Bridge for military purposes did the Old Bridge become a legitimate military target at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, like Monte Cassino and any other facility. It was a military target, but we -- I did not allow it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours, for the time that you've accorded me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. You said as using the maps that the Serbs had destroyed all bridges except for the Old Bridge. Why didn't they destroy the Old Bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hey, the man that they sent to activate the explosives inside the bridge, he -- he died. We killed him. The HVO killed him. And number two, the speed with which we were able to take the bridgehead off further down from the Old Bridge to the east, and my order to protect the Old Bridge against the mortar shells, that's what protected it. Exposing 40 people to a great deal of danger, I order that this cultural monument should be protected, and it was protected up to the last minute of my stay there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's almost 7.00 p.m. Tomorrow General Praljak's Defence needs some time to prepare for the additional questions that will heard on Thursday, but before Mr. Kovacic or Ms. Pinter has an opportunity to put questions to Mr. Praljak, the OTP will be asking questions based on the maps, and we shall finish Thursday with the additional questions. This is the best use of our time, and with that, I would like to wish you a pleasant evening, and we shall meet again and reconvene on Thursday at 2.15 p.m. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 10th day of September, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.56 p.m.,
